λεγόμενον· ὁ ζητῶν τὴν ἑαυτοῦ δόξαν οὐκ ἔστιν ἀληθινός, ὁ δὲ ζητῶν τὴν δόξαν τοῦ
πέμψαντος αὐτόν, οὗτος ἀληθής ἐστιν. Εἰ ἑαυτοὺς ἐκηρύσσομεν, ἦν ὑποπτεῦσαι ὅτι
δολοῦμεν τὸν λόγον, εἰ δὲ Χριστὸν καὶ τὴν αὐτοῦ δόξαν κηρύσσομεν, οὐδὲ εἷς δόλος
ἐν τῷ κηρύγματι. 2 Kor 4,6 Ἐν προσώπῳ Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ, ἀντὶ τοῦ διὰ Ἰησοῦν
Χριστόν, δι' ἐκεῖνον. Πρὸς φωτισμὸν τῆς γνώσεως, ὅτι ἡ γνῶσις οὐ λογισμοῖς
εὑρέθη, ἀλλὰ δι' ἀποκαλύψεως ἐξετέθη. Ἀντὶ τοῦ διὰ Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ ἔλαμψεν ἐν
ταῖς καρδίαις ἡμῶν, καὶ ἡ γνῶσις οὐ λογισμοῖς εὑρέθη, ἀλλὰ δι' ἀποκαλύψεως καὶ
ἐλλάμψεως ἐγνωρίσθη· οὐ γὰρ ἄν ποτε τούτου ἐφικέσθαι ἠδυνήθη ἄνθρωπος
σαρκίον περιβεβλημένος. 2 Kor 4,7–9 ∆είκνυσι διὰ τούτων καὶ τῶν ἑξῆς, ὅτι οὐ
συγχωρεῖ ὁ θεὸς πειρασθῆναι ὑπὲρ ὃ δυνάμεθα. εἰ γὰρ καὶ θλιβόμεθα ὑπὸ τῶν
διωκόντων, ἀλλ' οὐχ οὕτω στενοχωρούμεθα ὡς μηδαμοῦ ἔχειν ἀποφυγὴν καὶ
ἀπόκλισιν· πλατύνει γὰρ ὁ θεὸς τοῖς δι' εὐσέβειαν θλιβομένοις, ὅθεν καὶ ὁ ∆αυίδ
φησιν· ἐν θλίψει ἐπλάτυνάς με. 2 Kor 4,10 Τὴν νέκρωσιν ἀεὶ περιφέρομεν τῷ
κινδυνεύειν ἀεὶ διὰ Χριστὸν κοινωνοὶ τῶν παθημάτων τοῦ Χριστοῦ ὄντες. 289 2 Kor
4,11 Ὁ κύριος δι' ἡμᾶς εἰς θάνατον παρεδόθη, ἡμεῖς δὲ ὑπὲρ ἑαυτῶν διὰ Ἰησοῦν, ἵνα
κοινωνοὶ τῆς αὐτοῦ ζωῆς γενώμεθα. 2 Kor 4,12 ∆ιὰ τὸ κήρυγμα οἱ ἀπόστολοι
ἐκινδύνευον, ἐκήρυττον δὲ ἵνα ζήσωσιν οἱ πιστεύοντες, καὶ τοῦτό ἐστιν τὸ ἡ δὲ ζωὴ
ἐν ὑμῖν. 2 Kor 4,13 Ἐπειδή, φησί, πνεῦμα δουλείας ἐν τῷ νόμῳ, πνεῦμα δὲ υἱοθεσίας
ἐν τῇ χάριτι. εἶπε δὲ ὅτι τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ αὐτὸ ἔχομεν ὃ καὶ εἶχεν ὁ ∆αυίδ, προσέθηκε
τῆς πίστεως τὸ αὐτὸ πνεῦμα, οὐ τῆς νομικῆς δουλείας. Ἔχοντες, φησί, τὸ αὐτὸ
πνεῦμα τῷ ∆αυὶδ τῷ κατὰ πίστιν λαλήσαντι, καθὼς ἔφη· ἐπίστευσα, διὸ ἐλάλησα.
εἶτα εἰπὼν πνεῦμα προσέθηκε τῆς πίστεως· τοῦτο γὰρ κοινὸν νέας καὶ παλαιᾶς
μόνον, ἐπεὶ ἐν μὲν τῷ νόμῳ πνεῦμα ἦν δουλείας, ἐν δὲ τῇ χάριτι πνεῦμα υἱοθεσίας. 2
Kor 4,17–18 Εἰ θάνατοι καὶ κίνδυνοι καὶ πειρασμοὶ παρηκολούθουν, πῶς ἐλαφροτέρα
ἡ θλίψις; πῶς παραυτίκα; καὶ γὰρ παρέμειναν αὐτῷ οἱ πειρασμοὶ καὶ εἰς γῆρας
ἐλαύνοντο. πῶς οὖν ἐλαφρά ἐστιν ἡ θλίψις τῶν ἁγίων; ἢ δηλονότι ἀντεξαγομένη
πρὸς τὴν δόξαν τοῦ μέλλοντος αἰῶνος καὶ πρὸς τὰ προκείμενα ἀγαθὰ τοῖς δικαίοις·
πρὸς γὰρ ταῦτα καὶ βαρύτατοι πείρας μοι ἐλαφροὶ καταφαίνονται. καὶ οὐχ ἁπλῶς
ἐλαφραὶ αἱ θλίψεις ἀλλὰ καθ' ὑπερβολήν, αἵπερ θλίψεις πολὺ ὑστεροῦνται τοῦ
μεγέθους τῆς δόξης· τὸ γὰρ μέγα σῶμα καὶ βαρύ ἐστιν. ἢ καὶ βάρος εἶπεν κατὰ
μεταφορὰν τῶν σταθμίων· ἀντισταθμιζομένη γὰρ ταῖς θλίψεσιν ἡ δόξα βαρυτάτη
πάνυ εὑρίσκεται. παραυτίκα δὲ λέγει τὸ πρόσκαιρον· κἂν γὰρ μακρὰν ᾖ τὸ θλίβον καὶ
λυποῦν, ἀλλὰ πρόσκαιρον φαίνεται ὡς πρὸς τὸ τῆς δόξης ἀπέραντον. 2 Kor 5,1–2
Οἰκία σκήνους οὐ τὸ σκῆνος ἀλλ' ἡ οἰκία· ἡ γὰρ οἴκησις ἡ ἐνταῦθα παύεται, τὸ δὲ 290
σκῆνος ἀνίσταται. καὶ οἰκίαν εἶπε τὴν διαγωγὴν τήν τε θνητὴν καὶ τὴν
προσδοκωμένην. ἑξῆς μέντοι δείκνυσιν ὅτι οἰκητήριον λέγει τὴν φθορὰν καὶ τὴν
ἀφθαρσίαν. 289,ξολ2 Οἰκίαν σκήνους λέγει τὸ σῶμα, ὅπερ, φησίν, ἐὰν καὶ διαφθαρῇ
ἐν πειρασμοῖς καὶ κινδύνοις 290,ξολ2 διὰ Χριστόν, ἀποθησόμεθα αὐτὸ ὡς οἰκίαν
φθαρτὴν καὶ ἐν ἐσχάτῳ τῶν χειροποιήτων. εὑρήσομεν δὲ ἐν οὐρανοῖς ἑτέραν οἰκίαν
ἣν παρέχει ὁ θεὸς ἄφθαρτον καὶ ἀχειροποίητον. διὰ δὲ τούτων τήν τε θνητὴν
διαγωγὴν καὶ τὴν ἀθάνατον ἐμφαίνει. ∆ιὰ τοῦ ἐπενδύσασθαι δείκνυσιν ὅτι ἡ φθαρτὴ
σὰρξ ἀνίσταται καὶ τὴν ἀθάνατον ἐπενδύεται· ἡ γὰρ ἐπένδυσις λέγεται πρὸς ἑτέρῳ
ἐνδύματι. οἰκίαν δὲ δύο λέγει, τὴν θνητὴν καὶ τὴν προσδοκωμένην· καὶ δύο
οἰκητήρια, τὴν φθορὰν καὶ τὴν ἀφθαρσίαν, ὅτι τὸ μὲν ἀπολυόμεθα, τὸ δὲ
ἐπενδυόμεθα. οἰκητήριον δὲ λέγει τὸ ἐξ οὐρανοῦ τὴν ἐξ οὐρανῶν ἀφθαρσίαν, καθὸ
οὐκ ἔστι χειροποιητὴ ἀλλὰ θεοῦ δωρεά. 2 Kor 5,3 Πάντες μὲν δίκαιοι καὶ ἄδικοι
pass_a_gloss:
[Continues the 4:5 note from the previous section: "...not even one deceit is in the preaching, according to the] saying: the one seeking his own glory is not true, but the one seeking the glory of the one who sent him, this one is true.
[The Greek then repeats the 4:5 note as a second catena form: if we were preaching ourselves, it was possible to suspect that we falsify the word, but if we preach Christ and his glory, not even one deceit is in the preaching. It has no new material; not printed again.]
[Label 2 Cor 4:6.] "In the face of Jesus Christ," in place of "through Jesus Christ," on account of him. "Toward illumination of the knowledge": because the knowledge was not found by reasonings but was set out through revelation.
[Second form of the same note, not marked. Repeats: in place of "through Jesus Christ he shone in our hearts," and the knowledge was not found by reasonings but made known through revelation. New material:] and illumination; for a man clothed about with a bit of flesh could never have been able to reach this.
[Label 2 Cor 4:7-9.] He shows through these words and those following that God does not allow us to be tested beyond what we are able. For even if we are afflicted by those persecuting, yet we are not so hemmed in as to have nowhere escape and turning aside; for God makes room for those afflicted on account of godliness, whence David also says: "in affliction you made room for me."
[Label 2 Cor 4:10.] We always carry about the dying, by always being in danger on account of Christ, being sharers of the sufferings of Christ. [Page number 289 dropped.]
[Label 2 Cor 4:11.] The Lord was handed over to death on account of us, and we on behalf of ourselves on account of Jesus, so that we may become sharers of his life.
[Label 2 Cor 4:12.] On account of the preaching the apostles were in danger, but they were preaching so that those believing may live, and this is the "but life in you."
[Label 2 Cor 4:13.] Since, he says, a spirit of slavery is in the law, but a spirit of adoption in grace. And he said that we have the same spirit which David also had; he added "of faith," the same spirit, not that of the legal slavery.
[Second form of the same note, not marked. New material:] Having, he says, the same spirit as David, who spoke according to faith, just as he said: "I believed, therefore I spoke." [Repeats: then having said "spirit" he added "of faith";] for this alone is common to new and old, [repeats: since in the law there was a spirit of slavery, but in grace a spirit of adoption.]
[Label 2 Cor 4:17-18.] If deaths and dangers and trials followed along, how is the affliction lighter? How momentary? For the trials stayed with him and were driven on into old age. How then is the affliction of the saints light? Or clearly, being set against the glory of the coming age and toward the good things lying before the righteous; for toward these even the heaviest trials [Greek πείρας μοι, read as trials] appear light to me. And the afflictions are not simply light but beyond excess, since the afflictions fall far short of the greatness of the glory; for the great body is also heavy. Or he also said "weight" by metaphor from weights; for glory, weighed against the afflictions, is found exceedingly heavy. And he calls the temporary "momentary"; for even if the afflicting and grieving thing is long, yet it appears temporary as toward the endlessness of the glory.
[Label 2 Cor 5:1-2.] House of the tent: not the tent but the house; for the dwelling here ceases, but the tent rises. [Page number 290 dropped.] And he called house the way of life, both the mortal and the one expected. Next, however, he shows that by dwelling he means the corruption and the incorruption.
[Second catena form, marked 289 col. 2 and 290 col. 2. New material:] He calls the body house of the tent, which, he says, even if it is destroyed in trials and dangers on account of Christ, we will put off as a corruptible house and at the last of things made by hand. And we will find in the heavens another house, which God provides, incorruptible and not made by hand. [Repeats: and through these he indicates both the mortal way of life and the immortal.] Through the "to be clothed over" he shows that the corruptible flesh rises and puts on the immortal over it; for clothing-over is said on top of another garment. And he speaks of two houses, the mortal and the expected; and two dwellings, the corruption and the incorruption, because we are released from the one and we are clothed over with the other. And he calls the dwelling from heaven the incorruption from the heavens, in that it is not made by hand but a gift of God.
[Label 2 Cor 5:3.] All, on the one hand, righteous and unrighteous ... [continues in the next section]
pass_b_english: … saying: “Whoever seeks his own glory is not true, but whoever seeks the glory of the one who sent him is true” (John 7:18).

On 2 Corinthians 4:6: “In the face of Jesus Christ” stands for “through Jesus Christ,” that is, because of him. “For the illumination of the knowledge”: because this knowledge was not discovered by reasoning but laid open by revelation.
The second catena form adds: It was made known by revelation and illumination, for no human being wrapped in a scrap of flesh could ever have reached it.

On 2 Corinthians 4:7–9: By these words and the ones that follow he shows that God does not let us be tested beyond our strength (1 Corinthians 10:13). Persecutors may afflict us, but we are never so hemmed in that we have no escape and no way out anywhere; for God makes room for those afflicted for godliness' sake. That is why David says, “In affliction you made room for me” (Psalm 4:1).
On 2 Corinthians 4:10: We always carry about the dying because we are always in danger for Christ's sake, sharing in the sufferings of Christ.
On 2 Corinthians 4:11: The Lord was handed over to death for us; we are handed over for our own good, because of Jesus, so that we may come to share in his life.
On 2 Corinthians 4:12: Because of the preaching the apostles were in danger, yet they preached so that believers might live; that is what “but life in you” means.

On 2 Corinthians 4:13: For, he says, under the law there is a spirit of slavery, but under grace a spirit of adoption (Romans 8:15). He said that we have the same spirit that David had, and he added “of faith”: the same spirit of faith, not the slavery of the law.
The second catena form adds: We have the same spirit, he says, as David, who spoke by faith when he said, “I believed, therefore I spoke” (Psalm 116:10). This alone is common to the New and the Old.

On 2 Corinthians 4:17–18: If deaths, dangers and trials dogged him, how is the affliction “light”? How is it “momentary”? His trials stayed with him and pursued him into old age. How then is the affliction of the saints light? Or rather, it is plainly light when set against the glory of the age to come and the good things laid up for the righteous; beside these, even the heaviest trials seem light to me. The afflictions are not simply light but light beyond all measure, because they fall far short of the greatness of the glory; a large body is also a heavy one. Or else he spoke of “weight” by a metaphor from the scales: weighed against the afflictions, the glory proves very heavy indeed. By “momentary” he means temporary; for even if what afflicts and grieves us lasts long, it looks brief beside the endlessness of the glory.

On 2 Corinthians 5:1–2: “The house of the tent”: the house, not the tent; for our dwelling here comes to an end, while the tent rises again. By “house” he meant our way of life, both the mortal one and the one we wait for. Next, though, he shows that by “dwelling” he means corruption and incorruption.

The second catena form adds: By “the house of the tent” he means the body. Even if it is destroyed, he says, in trials and dangers for Christ's sake, we will lay it aside as a perishable house and the last of things made by hands, and we will find in heaven another house, which God provides, imperishable and not made by hands. By “to be clothed over” he shows that the perishable flesh rises and puts on immortality over itself; for one is said to be clothed over when a garment goes on top of another. He speaks of two houses, the mortal and the one we wait for, and of two dwellings, corruption and incorruption, because we are released from the one and clothed over with the other. By “the dwelling from heaven” he means the incorruption that comes from heaven, since it is not made by hands but is a gift of God.
On 2 Corinthians 5:3: All, both righteous and unrighteous, …
notes: 2026-11-11 claude-sumfix-b3: retranslated from the locked Greek. The old English was a word-order gloss, printed the 4:6 and 5:1-2 notes twice, and put '(2 Cor 4:7–9)' after words on 4:6. The section opens by finishing the 4:5 sentence begun at the end of u01-rem-close; the Greek then repeats the whole 4:5 note as an unmarked second form with nothing new, which is not printed again (the first form stands complete across the section break). Doublets collapsed: 4:6, 4:13 and 5:1-2 (first forms kept; new material printed under 'The second catena form adds:'). πείρας μοι read as 'trials'. Labels one per note (4:6 to 5:3); page and column marks dropped; section ends mid-sentence with '…'.

choices.why: The Greek begins by finishing the 4:5 sentence broken off at the end of u01-rem-close ('according to the | saying'). Nothing is moved between sections.

The Greek then prints the whole 4:5 note a second time (an unmarked second catena form) with nothing new; under the doublet rule the first form, complete across the section break, stands. Recorded here and in translator_notes.
The old English printed '(2 Cor 4:7–9)' after the 4:6 note; the edition's 4:6 label is used and 4:7-9 heads its own note.
